title: Against idleness
paragraphs: The Emperor Vespasian, when he was dying of the disease that killed him, did not for a moment stop asking about the state of the empire, and even from his bed kept dispatching a great many affairs of consequence. When his physician scolded him for this as harmful to his health, he replied: "An emperor must die standing." A fine line, in my opinion, and worthy of a great prince. The Emperor Hadrian later used the same words, and kings should often be reminded of them, so they understand that the great office of command over so many men is not a leisurely employment. There is nothing that can more justly disgust a subject and make him unwilling to expose himself to hardship and danger for his prince than seeing the prince meanwhile devoted to ease and trivial amusement, anxious for the safety of his own person while neglecting that of his people.

Anyone who wants to argue that it is better for a prince to conduct his wars through others rather than in his own person will easily find examples from fortune of lieutenants who have brought great enterprises to a happy end, and others whose master's presence did more harm than good. But no virtuous and valiant prince can stomach so dishonourable a counsel. Under the pretext of preserving his head for the happiness of his kingdom, like the statue of a saint, they degrade him and pronounce him incapable of the office he holds, which is military through and through. I know one prince who would rather be beaten than sleep while another fights for him, and who never hears without a touch of jealousy of any brave deed done by his own officers in his absence. And Suleiman I said, with very good reason in my view, that victories obtained without the master are never complete. He might have said more — that the master should blush with shame to claim any share of the honour, having contributed nothing to the work but his voice and his thought. Not even those, considering that in such work the only direction and command that earn honour are the ones given on the spot, in the heat of action. No pilot does his job standing still. The princes of the Ottoman house, the foremost in the world for military fortune, have warmly embraced this view, and Bajazet II, along with his son, who broke with it and spent their time on learning and other retired pursuits, struck heavy blows against their empire. Murad III, who now reigns, is following their example and beginning to feel the same effect. Was it not Edward III of England who said this of our Charles V: "There has never been a king who put on his armour so seldom, and yet never a king who gave me so much trouble." He had reason to find it strange, as an effect of chance more than reason. And let those who want to count the kings of Castile and Portugal among the warlike and magnanimous conquerors look for someone other than me to agree — because, from twelve hundred leagues away in their idle quarters, by the conduct of their captains, they made themselves masters of both Indies, of which it remains to be seen whether they would even have had the courage to go and enjoy them in person.

The Emperor Julian went still further, saying that a philosopher and a brave man ought not even to breathe — that is, not to grant the body any more than what cannot be refused, keeping the soul and body always intent and busy on honourable, great, and virtuous things. He was ashamed if anyone in public saw him spit or sweat — something also reported of the young men of Lacedaemon, and which Xenophon says of the Persians — because he believed that exercise, continual labour, and sobriety should have dried up all such surplus. What Seneca says fits here too: that the ancient Romans kept their young men always on their feet and taught them nothing they were to learn sitting down.

It is a generous wish to want to die usefully and like a man, but the outcome lies less in our resolution than in our luck. A thousand have set out in battle either to win or die, and have failed at both, wounds and imprisonment cutting across their plan and forcing them to live on against their will. There are diseases that overthrow even our wishes and our knowledge. Fortune was not bound to back up the vanity of the Roman legions, who swore by oath either to win or to die:
"Victor, Marce Fabi, revertar ex acie: si fallo, Jovem patrem, Gradivumque Martem aliosque iratos invoco deos."
["I will return, Marcus Fabius, a conqueror, from the fight: and if I fail, I invoke Father Jove, Mars Gradivus, and the other angry gods." — Livy, ii. 45.]

The Portuguese say that at one place during their conquest of the Indies, they met soldiers who had bound themselves by horrible curses to make no other deal but either to be killed or to remain victorious, and had shaved their heads and beards in token of this vow. There is little point in throwing ourselves forward and being obstinate: it seems as if blows avoid those who present themselves too eagerly, and refuse to fall on those who too willingly invite them, defeating their purpose. Some, after trying everything, unable for all their efforts to obtain the favour of dying by the enemy's hand, have been forced, to make good their resolution of either bringing home victory or losing their lives, to kill themselves in the very heat of the battle. There are other examples, but here is one: Philistus, general of the naval forces of the younger Dionysius against the Syracusans, offered them battle, which was sharply contested, the two sides being equal in strength. In this engagement he had the advantage at first, through his own valour; but when the Syracusans surrounded his galley to box him in, after having done great things in person to disengage himself and seeing no hope of relief, he took with his own hand the life he had so freely and uselessly exposed to the enemy.

Moulay Mohammed, king of Fez, who recently defeated Sebastian, king of Portugal, in the battle so famous for the death of three kings and the passing of that great kingdom to the crown of Castile, was extremely sick when the Portuguese entered his territory in arms. From that day on he grew steadily worse, drawing nearer to his end and foreseeing it. Yet no man ever used his remaining strength more vigorously and bravely than he did on that occasion. He felt too weak to undergo the pomp and ceremony of entering his camp, which in their fashion is magnificent, and so resigned that honour to his brother — but this was all of the general's role that he gave up. Everything else of any real use or necessity he carried out with exactness and glory, in his own person, his body stretched on a couch but his judgment and courage upright and firm to his last breath, and in a sense beyond it. He could have worn out his enemy, who had imprudently advanced into his territory, without striking a blow; and it was a very unfortunate circumstance that, for want of a little life or anyone to substitute in the conduct of the war and the affairs of a troubled state, he was driven to seek a doubtful and bloody victory when he already had a surer, better one in hand. Even so, he managed his lingering illness wonderfully, using it to wear out the enemy and to draw them far from the help of their fleet and the ports they held on the African coast, right up to the last day of his life, which he deliberately reserved for this great battle. He arranged his battalions in a circle, surrounding the Portuguese army on every side, and this circle closing in and drawing tight not only hindered the Portuguese in the fight — which was sharp enough thanks to the valour of the young invading king, since they had to present a front in every direction — but also blocked any flight after the defeat, so that, finding every exit held and shut by the enemy, they were forced to bunch up together again:
"Coacerventurque non solum caede, sed etiam fuga,"
["Piled up not only in slaughter but in flight."]

and there they were slain in heaps on top of one another, leaving the victor a bloody and complete victory. Dying, he had himself carried hurriedly from place to place wherever the need was greatest, and as he passed along the lines, he encouraged the captains and the soldiers one after another. When a corner of his main battalion was broken, there was no holding him from mounting his horse with his sword in his hand. He did his utmost to break free of those around him and rush into the thick of the battle, while they held him back, some by the bridle, some by his robe, others by his stirrups. This last effort completely drained what little life he had left. They laid him on his bed again, but coming to himself, starting as it were out of a swoon, with all other faculties failing him, to give his people notice that they were to conceal his death — the most necessary order he had left to give, so that his soldiers might not be discouraged by the news — he died with his finger pressed to his lips, the usual sign for silence. Who ever lived so long and so far into death? Who ever died more upright, or more like a man?

The most extreme form of facing death with courage, and the most natural, is to look upon it not only without alarm but without concern, continuing the usual course of life right into it, as Cato did, who occupied himself with his reading and went to sleep with a violent and bloody death in his heart and the weapon in his hand with which he had resolved to dispatch himself.
